cultivar: Chinary bushes (Camellia sinensis var. sinensis) from nineteenth-century seed
processing: Brief wither, then pan-firing or steaming to stop oxidation, rolling and drying in small factories; historically exported to Kashmir, Afghanistan and Central Asia.
harvest_season: April to October; the spring leaf is the gentlest and most prized.
taste_profile: Mild and sweetly vegetal with a nutty finish and very little bitterness.

brewing.notes: Forgiving for a green; keep the water around 80 °C and it will give a second steep.

vintage_note: Sold as the current season's harvest, mostly within northern India and at modest prices, with some going to Kashmir as the base for kahwa; a few speciality importers list spring lots by garden. Use within the year of harvest, kept sealed and dark.
description:
Kangra green tea is one of the two historic products of the Kangra valley in Himachal Pradesh. In the nineteenth century the valley's tea reached Kabul and Central Asia, and green tea went to Kashmir as well. Today it is the minority of the crop, about a tenth, and some of it still goes north to Kashmir for kahwa.

The leaf is withered briefly, then pan-fired or steamed to stop oxidation, rolled and dried; small factories around Palampur and a cooperative plant handle most of it. The Chinary bushes and cool mountain springs give a leaf that is naturally low in bitterness.

The cup is pale yellow-green, mild and sweetly vegetal with a nutty finish and almost no astringency, closer to a soft Chinese green than to anything from Japan. Brew it at around 80 °C for two to three minutes; it is forgiving, and a second steep works.

It is sold as the current season's harvest, with the spring lot the gentlest, mostly within northern India and at modest prices; a few speciality importers list it abroad under the garden name. Use it within the year of harvest, kept sealed and dark.

It makes a very good base for kahwa: simmer cardamom, cinnamon and a pinch of saffron in water, take it off the heat, then steep the green tea for a few minutes.
history:
Green tea has been made in Kangra alongside black since the mid-nineteenth century, from the Chinese variety planted after an 1848 survey. In the 1880s Kangra tea was being bought in Kabul and Central Asia, and the valley is known historically for exporting green tea to Kashmir and Afghanistan.

The 1905 earthquake ended the boom. Green is now the minority product, with black around 90 percent of output, but Kashmir still draws on the valley's green leaf for kahwah.
